deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page belongs to Gauss's magnetometric laboratory work of the early 1830s, around the absolute-intensity determination. The previous page determines moments of inertia from vibrations with added loads at two distances (231.4 mm and 20.0 mm). It gives a static moment of 15149, log 4.18037, and log moments of inertia for the needle with and without reinforcement. The next page continues deflection experiments with several needles placed W/N/E at 1.2 m.

Part 1 (dated May 2) records a weighing ('Eine Abwägung ergab'), all values in grams:
- Small magnet bar of dimensions 178.3 x 17.9 x 4.0 (presumably mm): 58.2 g.
- Mirror carrier (best read 'Spiegelträger ohne die kleine Feder', i.e. without the small spring): 67.4 g.
- The spring by itself: 1.1 g. So the carrier with spring would weigh 68.5 g (my addition).
- Sleeve including the brass hook: 17.4 g.
- Wooden rod: 35.3 g.
- Thick wire: 79 mm of length per 1 g, i.e. linear density 1/79 g/mm. My inference: if the wire is copper (rho ≈ 8.9 g/cm^3), the cross-section is about 1.42 mm^2 and the diameter about 1.35 mm.
- Silver dish: 3.4 g.

These masses are inputs for computing moments of inertia of the suspended system, as in the previous page.

Part 2 is a deflection (Ablenkung) experiment. The needle henceforth called D is suspended. Bars A, B, C are laid east and west of it at distance 1 m. Each row gives:
- the direction (O = east, W = west) of the north pole of the bar east of the needle and of the bar west of it;
- the mirror-scale reading;
- a 'Med.' column (about 158–159, slowly drifting to 157.7), apparently the mean or undisturbed position used to monitor drift.

In rows 1–4, C is east and B is west:
- (C W, B W) 51.5
- (C O, B W) 179.1
- (C O, B O) 264.9
- (C W, B O) 138.6

From row 5 on, A replaces B in the west position:
- (C W, A O) 193.5
- (C W, A W) unmeasurable (off scale)
- (C O, A W) 122.6
- (C O, A O) 319.4

The doubled deflection of a bar is the change in reading when that bar alone is reversed:
- B: 264.9 − 179.1 = 85.8 and 138.6 − 51.5 = 87.1. Mean 86.45, as recorded.
- C: 179.1 − 51.5 = 127.6, 264.9 − 138.6 = 126.3, and 319.4 − 193.5 = 125.9. Mean 379.8/3 = 126.6, as recorded.
- A: 319.4 − 122.6 = 196.8, as recorded (only one usable pair).

The sign convention is consistent with the end-on ('first principal') position: a bar on either side with its north pole east pushes the reading up. Since all bars are at the same distance, the doubled deflections 196.8 : 86.45 : 126.6 give, to first order, the ratio of the magnetic moments of A : B : C relative to H.

My own check of the 'unmeasurable' entry: additivity predicts 193.5 − 196.8 = −3.3, below the scale zero, which explains 'unmessb.' Similarly, 122.6 − 126.6 ≈ −4 or 51.5 − 86.45 + 196.8 − ... also falls off scale.

Non-additivity is small. The mean of the like-pole pair (51.5 + 264.9)/2 = 158.2 differs from the mean of the mixed pair (179.1 + 138.6)/2 = 158.85. This is consistent with drift (see the Med. column) and tangent nonlinearity.
errors: No arithmetic errors: 86.45, 126.6 and 196.8 all check exactly from the readings.

The 'Med.' column values (158.025, 159.025, ...) cannot be reproduced as simple means of the listed readings. They are presumably independently observed rest or mean positions, so their role is uncertain.

Possible inconsistency, not necessarily Gauss's error: if the bar's dimensions are 178.3 x 17.9 x 4.0 mm and it is steel (about 7.8 g/cm^3), it should weigh about 99.6 g, not 58.2 g. The implied density is about 4.56 g/cm^3. Either a dimension is misread or not in mm, or the figures mean something else.
The A reversal rests on a single pair, since the other pair was off scale, so A's value is less well determined than B's and C's.

results.what: Weighing of the components of the suspended magnetometer system (magnet bar, mirror carrier, spring, sleeve with brass hook, wooden rod, wire linear density, silver dish) for moment-of-inertia computations
results.modern_name: Mass inventory for moment-of-inertia determination of a torsion/magnetometer suspension
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Intensitas vis magneticae terrestris ad mensuram absolutam revocata, 1832/33)

results.what: Deflection method with reversal of deflecting bars in east/west end-on positions at a fixed distance of 1 m; doubled deflections give relative magnetic moments of bars A, B, C
results.modern_name: Gauss deflection method (first Gauss position, tangent/end-on position) with commutation by magnet reversal

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine laboratory notes from Gauss's well-documented magnetometric programme: weighings and a reversal-deflection experiment comparing bar moments. The methods are exactly those published in Intensitas (1832) and the Resultate; nothing new mathematically.

checkable.asserts: Mean doubled deflection of B from the two reversal pairs equals 86.45
Mean doubled deflection of C from three reversal pairs equals 126.6
Predicted reading for (C W, A W) is -3.3, i.e. off scale, consistent with 'unmessb.'
A steel bar of 178.3x17.9x4.0 mm would weigh about 99.6 g, versus the recorded 58.2 g (dimension/units question)
Assuming copper, a wire of 79 mm per gram has diameter about 1.35 mm
Mirror carrier plus small spring weighs 68.5 g (if the carrier reading is 'ohne die kleine Feder')

transcription_corrections: 'Spiegelträgerrohr die kleine Feder' is better read 'Spiegelträger ohne die kleine Feder' (mirror carrier without the small spring). This fits the next line, 'diese Feder für sich'.
The first dimension of the small magnet bar shows an overwritten digit (178.3, with 8 apparently written over 7).
'die Hülse incl. des Messingenen Hakes' is probably 'des messingenen Hakens'.
'Distanz 1^m' is spelled 'Distanz' in the manuscript; the meaning is 1 metre.
In the row 'W A O', 'A' is a marginal label showing that from this row on bar A replaces B in the West position; it is not a pole direction.
The header is 'Hieraus doppelter Ausschlag', with 'einfacher' struck out; the 'von' belongs before C.
